ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 5 — Preventive Visit — Calamity Jane

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

text.paragraph: Ms. Canary is a 44-year-old woman with severe alcohol use disorder in early remission on monthly extended-release naltrexone, and alcohol-associated steatotic liver disease, who comes for her yearly preventive visit four weeks after her four-week review; her second naltrexone injection is due today. She has had no alcohol since intake, eight weeks ago. She has had the urge to drink on a few evenings and called the peer recovery specialist twice. Her tooth socket has healed. She is eating two meals a day with SNAP benefits and has gained weight. She is still staying at her friend's house and is on the waiting list for a room through the housing program. She cannot remember a Pap test or a mammogram, or any vaccines as an adult. [S]

tr.td: Thin, well; weight 51.4 kg, BMI 18.9; blood pressure 120/76; pulse 76

Alcohol use disorder, severe (nine of eleven DSM-5-TR criteria), daily drinking of about a pint of whiskey with heavier binges for many years; synthetic modern episode linked to her documented lifelong heavy drinking
S — Synthetic modern coding; DSM-5-TR severe alcohol use disorder maps to F10.20 when withdrawal is coded separately. Person-first language; not a claim about her real diagnosis.
Alcohol withdrawal, mild, at low risk of complications (PAWSS 3, CIWA-Ar 9 at intake; no past seizures or delirium tremens), managed as an outpatient with daily nurse checks
S — Synthetic withdrawal episode; resolved by the one-week visit.
Raised liver enzymes (AST 96, ALT 44, GGT 240 U/L) with a FIB-4 index of 3.93, above the cut point for possible advanced fibrosis; liver stiffness measurement planned
S — Synthetic presenting finding; superseded when elastography and the clinical picture supported alcohol-associated steatotic liver disease.
Alcohol-associated steatotic liver disease, without cirrhosis: liver stiffness 9.6 kPa after four weeks without alcohol, falling enzymes, normal bilirubin, albumin, INR and platelets
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the four-week visit.
Depressive symptoms during heavy drinking (PHQ-9 14, item 9 scored 0); whether they are alcohol-induced or an independent depression to be judged after two to four weeks without alcohol
S — Synthetic provisional finding; resolved as the PHQ-9 fell to 5 after ten weeks without alcohol, consistent with alcohol-induced depressive symptoms. Not a claim about her real mood.
Daily chewing tobacco for many years; not ready to stop at intake
S — Synthetic modern coding anchored to the documented chewing tobacco.
Underweight (BMI 18.4) with poor food intake, low folate, magnesium and phosphate, and slightly low albumin
S — Synthetic finding anchored to a contemporary impression of poor nutrition (R).
Housing instability: staying in a spare room at a friend's house, with nowhere to go if that ends; has stayed in shelters in past winters
S — Synthetic social need anchored to her documented poverty and moves from town to town.
Food insecurity: often goes without meals at the end of the month
S — Synthetic social need anchored to her documented poverty.

S — Synthetic acute illness; not a historical claim.

Guideline basis: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); Medicare Preventive Services reference: visit templates, screening cascades, and documentation elements (2026); USPSTF A and B Recommendations (2026); Adult Immunization Schedule by Age (2026)

Follow-up: Ten-week review in two weeks. HPV, tuberculosis test and mammogram results at the next visits. Second hepatitis B dose in one month or more; second hepatitis A dose in six months. Naltrexone injection at a nurse visit in four weeks. Next preventive visit in one year. Next scheduled visit 2026-05-11: ten-week review: recovery, mood, housing and results. [S]

Voluntary advance care planning discussion of about 16 minutes, with her consent. She named a health care agent, the friend she is staying with, and a health care proxy form was completed; the agent is recorded in the chart and is not named here. She said that what matters most to her is her independence and her friends, and that she wants to be told the truth about her health in plain words. She chose not to record specific treatment preferences today. The plan will be revisited yearly or after any serious illness. [S]
